canonical_fact: JAM is a permissionless protocol combining a global singleton service environment with secure parallel in-core computation and on-chain state transition.
misconceptions: JAM is simply an Ethereum-style smart-contract chain.

relations.statement: JAM exposes its programmable global environment through services.

title: JAM

canonical_fact: JAM separates high-throughput largely stateless in-core computation from stateful on-chain accumulation.
misconceptions: All JAM service computation happens synchronously on-chain.

relations.statement: Refine is the primary in-core entry point.
Accumulate is the stateful on-chain entry point.

title: In-core/on-chain dualism

canonical_fact: A JAM blockchain is defined by a genesis state and a deterministic block-level state-transition function mapping prior state and a valid block to posterior state.
misconceptions: JAM state may change nondeterministically as long as validators agree.
title: Block-level state transition

canonical_fact: The genesis state is the agreed initial state from which all later canonical states are derived by repeated valid state transitions.
title: Genesis state

canonical_fact: A JAM block consists of a header plus extrinsic input data that drives the block-level state transition.

relations.statement: A JAM block is composed of the header plus extrinsic data.

title: Block

canonical_fact: JAM block extrinsic data is partitioned into tickets, disputes, preimages, assurances and guarantees/reports.
title: Extrinsic data

canonical_fact: JAM exposes permissionless programmable services rather than restricting computation to a single fixed application.

relations.statement: A service has protocol-visible account state including code identity, storage and balance.

title: Service model

canonical_fact: Coretime is JAM's resource for resilient computational capacity on cores; authorization separates its assignment from the exact work package that later uses it.
misconceptions: Coretime is exactly the same object as Ethereum transaction gas.

relations.statement: The authorization system is what decouples coretime assignment from a specific workload.

title: Coretime

canonical_fact: Validators are privileged protocol participants that help author blocks and perform guaranteeing, availability and auditing duties.
misconceptions: Validators only author blocks and have no role in work availability or auditing.

relations.statement: Safrole selects validators for block-authoring opportunities by timeslot.
Guarantors are validators performing the initial work-report correctness role.

title: Validator

canonical_fact: A core is a parallel work-execution resource whose authorization state and current work-report availability assignment are tracked by JAM.
misconceptions: A JAM core is just a validator CPU core and has no protocol-level identity.

relations.statement: Each core has its own authorizer pool controlling which work may use that core.

title: Core

canonical_fact: JAM uses deterministic gas accounting to bound PVM execution; gas values are unsigned 64-bit quantities.
misconceptions: Gas in JAM is a floating market price rather than deterministic execution accounting.
title: Gas

canonical_fact: The PVM is JAM's RISC-V-based virtual machine used to execute permissionless service logic deterministically.
misconceptions: The PVM is the EVM with a different opcode table.

relations.statement: PVM code interacts with JAM through protocol-defined host calls rather than arbitrary OS access.

title: Polkadot Virtual Machine

canonical_fact: For a valid block, deterministic state transition defines a unique state; fork-choice and finality mechanisms are used to converge on canonical history.
title: Canonical history

canonical_fact: A fork occurs when multiple valid blocks reference the same prior block, creating competing heads with distinct states.
title: Fork

canonical_fact: A finalized block is one considered with extremely high confidence to remain permanently in canonical history, together with all its ancestors.
title: Finalized block
